intro: VialGrade is a research platform I built for the peptide market that aggregates public data from batches, COAs, lab reports, test results, vendors, and other sources into one place, then grades vendors and storefronts against a rubric so you can see what the grade is based on.
orientation: A friend of mine is really into biomedicine and peptide research, and that got me looking at the market. I realized pretty quickly how hard it was to compare vendor claims against public records, COAs, lab reports, and independent testing, so I started building one place to organize that evidence.
origin: They all seemed to say they had verified certificates and high purity, but even when there was a document on the page, I didn't know whether it belonged to that particular batch or company, and it was hard to compare one vendor with another when each site was presenting its own information.

I thought I could use AI and software to cross-check some of that, so I started building VialGrade around the lab reports, which are called certificates of analysis, or COAs, and matching the batch and company information so someone could follow a claim back to the record behind it.
unknown: One thing I had to figure out was what to do when there wasn't enough information, because not finding a lab record doesn't mean the vendor did something wrong, and I didn't want the software giving someone a bad grade just because I hadn't collected enough data on them yet.
grading: The grade looks at independent testing, regulatory records, and information about the business, so a documented problem can still affect the grade even if other records look good, while a vendor without enough evidence can be left ungraded rather than pretending there is information to support that grade when there isn't.
handoff: I originally wanted people to be able to check out through VialGrade, but I couldn't make that work, so I ended up linking to the vendor's page instead and then had to figure out how to keep track of what happened when someone left the site.
attribution: I added tracking tags and a short VialGrade click reference to those links so I could track the handoff and the destination could identify where the traffic came from, although a click still doesn't tell me whether the person actually bought anything.
earlyUse: In an early update I had around 2,000 Google impressions, about 600 clicks into the site, and eight signups over a month, which honestly surprised me because it meant people I didn't know were finding something I'd built and actually using it.
takeaway: The main thing I wanted was one place where someone could look at a vendor's claim, see the records behind it, and understand why it got the grade it did. The part I still have to be careful about is missing data, because if I don't have enough information, I would rather say that than make the grade look more certain than it is.
